Naval Drills Raise Fears of a Wider Indo-Pacific Crisis China's expanding naval activity around Taiwan is raising concerns that Beijing is rehearsing ways to isolate the island and prevent the United States and its regional allies from intervening in a potential conflict.
China’s expanding naval activity around Taiwan is raising concerns that Beijing is rehearsing ways to isolate the island and prevent the United States and its regional allies from intervening in a potential conflict. The latest movements by Chinese warships across the Taiwan Strait and the Western Pacific have intensified fears of a possible blockade, while encouraging Washington, Tokyo, Canberra and Manila to strengthen military coordination.
The developments also highlight a growing strategic contest extending beyond Taiwan itself. Beijing’s military pressure is testing regional security arrangements, while Taipei is working to convince international partners that defending the island is essential to protecting global technology supply chains, particularly the semiconductor industry.
Late last month, Taiwan reported that dozens of Chinese warships from the Eastern, Northern and Southern Theatre commands had begun operating around the island and across the Western Pacific, including movements towards the US territory of Guam. Taipei described the activity as an obvious threat.
Unlike previous large-scale Chinese military exercises, which were often accompanied by official announcements, television coverage and warnings against Taiwanese independence, Beijing described the latest movements as routine training that was not directed against any particular country.

Taiwan’s Defence Minister Wellington Koo subsequently characterised the operations as “area denial drills”. The objective, according to Taipei, is to demonstrate China’s ability to prevent US and allied forces from reaching Taiwan if Beijing launches an attack.
The distinction between conventional military exercises and area denial operations is strategically important. Rather than focusing exclusively on an amphibious invasion, China could seek to restrict access to Taiwan through naval deployments, air operations and pressure on surrounding maritime routes.
Such a strategy could complicate any attempt by the United States or its partners to provide military assistance. A blockade would also have serious economic consequences, potentially disrupting commercial shipping, energy supplies and the movement of advanced semiconductors.
The Washington-based Institute for the Study of War has suggested that China’s recent military activity could demonstrate its ability to impose a blockade whenever it chooses. Its assessment comes as the United States remains heavily engaged in the Middle East and Ukraine, while dealing with the political consequences of its midterm elections.
Nevertheless, regional officials and analysts are not generally predicting an immediate Chinese military operation. China’s military command structure is still recovering from the dismissal of numerous senior generals in late 2025 and early 2026, raising questions about the readiness and internal stability of its leadership.
Beijing has never renounced the use of force to bring Taiwan under its control, although it continues to state a preference for peaceful reunification. Taiwan rejects China’s sovereignty claims and maintains its own democratic political system.
The latest naval movements therefore serve both operational and political purposes. They demonstrate military capabilities while increasing pressure on Taiwan and its potential international supporters.
Taipei is also pursuing a diplomatic strategy designed to make international partners more conscious of the consequences of a conflict.
Over the past year, Taiwan’s government has intensified efforts to persuade policymakers and corporate leaders, particularly in the United States, that the island remains indispensable to global supply chains. Its semiconductor industry is central to this argument.
Despite American efforts to diversify advanced chip production by encouraging investment outside Taiwan, the global artificial intelligence boom has reinforced the island’s importance. Demand for sophisticated processors and semiconductor manufacturing capacity has made Taiwan an increasingly significant part of the international technology economy.
Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing Company (TSMC), the world’s leading contract chipmaker, has committed substantial investment to new facilities in the United States and Germany. These projects are intended partly to reduce the risks associated with concentrating production on an island exposed to geopolitical tensions.
However, Taiwanese officials argue that overseas factories cannot immediately replace the industrial capabilities and technological ecosystem developed at home.
Foreign Minister Lin Chia-lung reinforced this position in a November 3 article in Foreign Affairs , arguing that Taiwan’s future would help determine whether democracies or authoritarian governments shape the standards and values of the emerging digital age.
He also described Taiwan’s semiconductor industry as a strategic asset for the United States in its competition with China over artificial intelligence.
This argument reflects Taipei’s effort to connect its security directly with American economic and technological interests. The more dependent international companies become on Taiwanese manufacturing, the greater the potential global consequences of a conflict.
China’s growing military presence has encouraged regional powers to improve their ability to coordinate in a crisis.
Following a meeting of the grouping known as the Squad in Manila late last month, the United States, Australia, the Philippines and Japan agreed to establish a Combined Coordination Center. The arrangement, announced this week, is intended to improve joint planning among the four countries in the event of a conflict around Taiwan.
The initiative reflects growing concern that a crisis could quickly involve several countries, particularly if Chinese operations threaten regional maritime routes or military facilities.
The US Indo-Pacific Command has repeatedly identified deterring Chinese military action against Taiwan as a central priority. American planners have also explored the use of unmanned systems to create what they describe as a “hellscape” of obstacles that would make a Chinese military advance extremely costly.
However, military preparation does not automatically guarantee American intervention. The decision would ultimately rest with the US president.
President Donald Trump has repeatedly questioned why Washington should defend Taiwan, creating uncertainty about the future of American commitments. His position contrasts with the more explicit assurances offered by former President Joe Biden, who repeatedly said the United States would come to Taiwan’s defence if it were attacked.
This uncertainty complicates regional deterrence. US allies may strengthen their military coordination, but they still need clarity about the extent of American support in a crisis.
The Pentagon’s continued exercises and deployments suggest that operational preparations remain a priority despite Washington’s other international commitments. However, concerns about the availability of air defence and strike missiles illustrate the resource pressures facing the US military.
China’s military activity is also affecting relations with neighbouring countries. Japan has adopted a more assertive position under Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi, who has described a potential Chinese attack on Taiwan as a threat to Japan’s survival.
Her comments and increased Japanese military spending have angered Beijing, which regards Taiwan as an internal matter and opposes foreign involvement.
For Tokyo, however, the security of Taiwan is closely connected to the protection of nearby maritime routes and the defence of Japan’s southwestern islands. A conflict could threaten regional shipping and place Japanese territory and US military facilities in the region under pressure.
The Philippines also has direct security concerns because of its proximity to Taiwan and its growing defence cooperation with Washington. Together, these developments have strengthened incentives for regional military coordination.
Taiwan is simultaneously expanding less formal partnerships. On November 6, Australia’s senior representative in its de facto embassy in Taipei met Geological Survey and Mining Management Agency Director Hsu Ming-hong to discuss critical minerals.
Such contacts demonstrate that cooperation is extending beyond traditional defence issues into areas involving strategic resources and economic security.
Even without an invasion, a deliberate Chinese blockade could produce serious economic disruption. Taiwan is a major semiconductor producer, while China, Japan and South Korea occupy central positions in global manufacturing and technology supply chains.
A prolonged confrontation could interrupt exports to Europe, Australia and other developed economies, affecting industries that depend on advanced chips, electronics and manufactured components.
Businesses are increasingly recognising these risks. Companies in Australia are offering exercises and training to help organisations assess how they would maintain supply chains during a conflict or blockade involving Taiwan.
TSMC’s overseas investment provides one form of protection, but it does not eliminate the vulnerability. Building additional semiconductor facilities takes time, and manufacturing capacity cannot be transferred immediately without significant technical and commercial challenges.
The risks also extend into the competition over critical minerals. China’s restrictions on rare earths and other important exports during last year’s trade confrontation with Washington demonstrated how economic dependencies can become instruments of geopolitical pressure.
Analysts have described Beijing’s broader response as the development of a “fortress economy”, in which China seeks to strengthen its position as a supplier of advanced products while reducing dependence on vulnerable external resources and relationships.
This approach adds another dimension to the Taiwan dispute. A conflict would not simply involve military forces; it could also expose the vulnerabilities of an interconnected global economy.
Although Taiwan is strengthening ties with several countries, its diplomatic position remains complicated.
Some regional governments are reluctant to become involved in the growing confrontation between Beijing and Taipei. Papua New Guinea ended its relations with Taiwan this year, while Taiwanese officials suspended technological cooperation with Malaysia after Kuala Lumpur adopted a stricter interpretation of Beijing’s one-China policy.
These developments demonstrate that China’s diplomatic influence continues to constrain Taiwan’s international engagement.
However, Beijing’s military pressure can also produce unintended consequences. A Chinese submarine-launched ballistic missile test in the South Pacific in July prompted several Pacific island countries to deepen relations with the United States and Australia.
Taiwan is also developing links with European partners. This month, Taiwanese drone company AerosoarX announced a cooperation agreement with Ukrainian-British firm UFORCE. The European company highlighted Taiwan’s importance in reducing dependence on supply chains dominated by China.
Such partnerships illustrate how the strategic competition involving Taiwan increasingly overlaps with wider debates about defence technology, industrial resilience and the relationship between democratic governments.
The immediate question is whether China’s latest naval movements represent routine military activity or a more deliberate effort to demonstrate its ability to isolate Taiwan. The answer may become clearer through future deployments, the scale of regional exercises and the extent of coordination between Beijing’s military commands.
Taiwan’s 2028 elections could also become an important political milestone. Some regional officials and analysts believe a deliberate blockade is unlikely before then, although this remains an assessment rather than a confirmed timeline. Beijing’s relationship with Taiwan’s political opposition, particularly the Kuomintang and its leader Cheng Li-wun, may influence the diplomatic environment.
Meanwhile, the expected meeting between Trump and Chinese President Xi Jinping on the sidelines of the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation summit in Shenzhen could provide an opportunity to address regional tensions. Whether Taiwan features prominently in their discussions remains uncertain.
For Washington and its allies, the challenge is to strengthen deterrence without creating conditions that make military confrontation more likely. For Taipei, the priority is to maintain international support while demonstrating that its security is closely tied to the stability of global technology and trade networks.
China’s latest naval activity sends a message that extends far beyond the Taiwan Strait. Beijing is demonstrating its ability to challenge regional military arrangements, pressure neighbouring governments and exploit economic dependencies. Whether these operations remain demonstrations of strength or develop into a more dangerous confrontation will shape the security and economic future of the Indo-Pacific.
